title: The pilgrimages
hook: tradition says he traveled with Sikhs to pilgrim sites and spoke against the pilgrim tax

segments.voice: Yesterday, the manjis: plain seats where teachers, women and men, held the sangat near home. Your line was spread it far.

Pay here before you pray. A gate at the edge of a holy river, and someone collecting a fee from every traveler who wants to bathe. A family has walked for days. They're tired, they've saved for this, and now there's a charge just to reach the water. Sikh tradition tells of Guru Amar Das traveling with his Sikhs to pilgrim places, the crowded river towns where people came to bathe and remember God. And it remembers him speaking up about a tax laid on the pilgrims themselves.
screen: `PAY HERE BEFORE YOU PRAY.` → `A FAMILY AT THE RIVER GATE.` → `THE GURU AMONG THE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: Why would a Guru go to a pilgrim town at all? The Sikh Gurus taught that the true pilgrimage is inward. Guru Nanak puts it plainly in the Japji, paraphrased: I would bathe at the place of pilgrimage if that pleased Him; without pleasing Him, what good is the bathing? The Sikh word for a pilgrim place is tirath, and the Japji itself speaks of bathing at a tirath within. So Sikh tellings present it this way: he went where the people already were. Seekers gathered there, hungry for God, and the Guru met them in the crowd, sang the Word, and fed people. Not to mock their journey, but to share what the Gurus had found. Then the tax. Tradition says the Guru spoke against a charge laid on pilgrims, and some accounts say the emperor Akbar later lifted it. Whatever the details, the instinct runs through the stories of his time: no one should have to pay to come near God. Tradition says the well at Goindval was open to every caste. The langar row asks no fee. The Guru's Word is sung for anyone who walks in. A tax on pilgrims put a price on the very thing the Gurus kept giving away. So the line has two sides: free pilgrims from unfair charges, and remember that the pilgrimage inward needs no gate at all.
screen: `TIRATH: THE PLACE OF PILGRIMAGE.` · `HE WENT WHERE THE PEOPLE WERE.` · `NO PRICE TO COME NEAR GOD.` · `THE PILGRIMAGE WITHOUT A GATE.` · then, large: `FREE PILGRIMS.`

segments.voice: Think of a cost someone has to pay just to belong, worship, learn or be helped, a fee, a form, a rule, a look at the door, in your workplace, your town or your own house. Hold it without anger and ask simply: who does this keep out, and does it need to? Then let the breath carry you to the tirath within that the Japji speaks of, and if you pray, say Waheguru there.
The pilgrimages. Guru Amar Das, tradition says, went among the pilgrims, shared the Word, and spoke against a tax that charged them to come near God. Today's word.
Your line: free pilgrims. No one should have to pay to come near God. Until tomorrow, then.

howItsDone: Sikhs tell the stories of Guru Amar Das's journeys and the pilgrim tax in histories and katha, and they speak of an inward pilgrimage; gurdwaras are open to visitors without any fee.

chat.says: If Sikhs see pilgrimage as inward, why did Guru Amar Das go to pilgrim towns?
options: To meet seekers where they already were, sharing the Word and food, not mocking them.
To leave the busy crowds behind and live as a quiet hermit beside the rivers.
To collect the pilgrim tax himself and use it to pay for the langar.
